entities.name: Abd al-Rahim al-Hajj Muhammad
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abd al-Rahim al-Hajj Muhammad Al Saif, known by his kunya Abu Kamal, emerged as a pivotal Palestinian Arab commander during the tumultuous 1936–1939 Arab Revolt, a violent uprising against the British Mandate for Palestine and the accelerating Zionist settlement. Operating primarily across the northern West Bank districts of Tulkarm, Nablus, and Jenin, his leadership galvanized thousands of rural Palestinians and former Ottoman soldiers, transforming localized grievances into a coordinated, if ultimately unsuccessful, national resistance movement. His rise to prominence in the mid-1930s underscored the escalating tensions between Arab aspirations for self-determination and the British commitment to facilitate a Jewish national home, placing him at the heart of one of the most significant anti-colonial struggles in the interwar Middle East.

Al-Hajj Muhammad's military career during the revolt was marked by both strategic ingenuity and tactical ferocity. Initially leading local guerrilla bands, he quickly expanded his influence, organizing attacks on British military installations, Jewish settlements, and infrastructure like roads and pipelines. By September 1938, as the revolt reached its zenith, he was appointed General Commander, a role he shared rotationally with other key figures such as Arif Abd al-Raziq, reflecting the decentralized, yet increasingly unified, command structure of the rebel forces. His campaigns often involved hit-and-run tactics, leveraging the mountainous terrain to evade British patrols and inflict casualties, thereby maintaining constant pressure on the Mandate authorities and frequently disrupting the British administration.
